objectives: Describe the structure of the Earth and the movement of plates
Distinguish constructive, destructive and conservative boundaries
Link boundaries to landforms, earthquakes and volcanoes
reviewNotes: Plate speeds are given only as ‘a few centimetres a year’; check the figure used in the official syllabus.

blocks.title: Plates
blocks.md: The **lithosphere** (crust and top of the mantle) is broken into rigid **plates**. They move slowly, a few centimetres a year, over the hotter, softer **asthenosphere**. Causes include convection currents in the mantle, **ridge push** and **slab pull** (a cold, dense plate sinking pulls the rest of the plate with it).

blocks.title: Three kinds of boundary
blocks.md: **Constructive (divergent):** plates move apart, magma rises, new crust forms (mid-ocean ridges, rift valleys). **Destructive (convergent):** plates move together; a dense oceanic plate is **subducted** (trenches, fold mountains, volcanoes, strong earthquakes). **Conservative (transform):** plates slide past each other; earthquakes but no crust created or destroyed.

blocks.caption: The three types of plate boundary (schematic).
blocks.alt: Three small diagrams with arrows: constructive boundary with plates moving apart, destructive with plates moving together, conservative with plates sliding past.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Volcanoes and earthquakes are not only found at plate edges: hot spots and other zones exist.
- Mount Cameroon lies on the Cameroon Volcanic Line, which is not a simple plate boundary and whose origin is still discussed by geologists.
- Plates move, continents do not ‘float’ separately from them.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Identify the boundary
blocks.statement: Plate A (oceanic) and plate B (continental) are moving towards each other. Name the boundary, the process and two landforms or hazards.
steps: Plates moving together form a destructive boundary.
The denser oceanic plate A sinks beneath B: this is subduction.
Landforms: an ocean trench and fold mountains or a chain of volcanoes on plate B.
Hazards: powerful earthquakes and explosive eruptions.
blocks.answer: Destructive boundary; subduction; trench, volcanoes/fold mountains; earthquakes and eruptions.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Explain a rift valley
blocks.statement: East Africa has long, steep-sided valleys with lakes and volcanoes. Explain how plate movement can produce them.
steps: Where the crust is pulled apart (a divergent setting), it is stretched and thinned.
Blocks of crust between faults drop down and form a rift valley with steep sides.
Magma rises through the weak crust and builds volcanoes.
Shallow earthquakes occur as the faults move.
blocks.answer: Stretching and faulting drop blocks to form the valley; rising magma gives volcanoes and earthquakes.

blocks.title: Weathering
blocks.md: **Weathering** is the breakdown of rock **in place**, with no transport. **Erosion** involves a moving agent (water, wind, ice). **Physical** weathering breaks rock without changing its minerals (heating and cooling, freeze-thaw, salt crystals). **Chemical** weathering changes minerals (carbonation, hydrolysis, oxidation). **Biological** weathering is caused by roots, burrowing animals and lichens.

blocks.title: Weathering in warm, wet climates
blocks.md: Chemical reactions speed up with heat and water, so in the humid tropics rocks decay to great depths, forming thick weathered layers and clay-rich soils. In hot deserts temperature changes and salt crystals dominate. Freeze-thaw needs repeated frost, so it is rare in the lowland tropics.

items.text: Heavy rain and cleared slopes raise the risk

blocks.caption: Slope processes: steeper slopes favour rapid movement.
blocks.alt: Slope profile showing a steep upper part with rockfalls and landslides and a gentle lower part with soil creep.

blocks.title: Mass movement
blocks.md: **Mass movement** is the downslope movement of weathered material under gravity. It ranges from slow **soil creep** to **mudflows**, **slumps**, **landslides** and **rockfalls**. Triggers: steep slope, heavy rain that saturates soil, loss of vegetation, undercutting by rivers or roads, and earthquakes.

blocks.title: Weathering is not erosion
blocks.md: Do not write that rivers ‘weather’ the valley: rivers erode. Landslides have occurred on steep, built-up hillsides in Cameroon during heavy rain, so slope management matters for planning.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Name the type
blocks.statement: Rock containing limestone is dissolved slowly by rainwater that has absorbed carbon dioxide. Name the process and the group of weathering it belongs to.
steps: Rainwater with dissolved CO₂ is a weak acid.
It reacts with calcium carbonate: this is carbonation.
A chemical change takes place, so it is chemical weathering.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Explain a landslide
blocks.statement: A steep hillside was cleared of trees for housing. After days of rain a section slid downhill. Explain why.
steps: Roots held the soil together and trees intercepted rain; both were lost.
Rainfall filled the soil pores, adding weight and reducing friction between particles.
On a steep slope gravity then overcame the strength of the material.
Cutting into the slope for houses removed support at the base.
blocks.answer: Loss of vegetation, saturation, steepness and undercutting triggered the movement.

reviewNotes: Hydrograph reading skills: confirm whether the syllabus expects drainage-basin systems diagrams.
Case studies of local rivers (Wouri, Sanaga, Benue) to be chosen by the teacher; no statistics given.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Processes
blocks.md: **Erosion:** hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution. **Transport:** solution, suspension, saltation and traction (rolling). **Deposition** happens when velocity falls, for example at a bend, in a lake or at the mouth. Larger load needs faster flow; flow is fastest in flood.

blocks.title: Landforms along the long profile
blocks.md: **Upper course:** steep, V-shaped valley, rapids, waterfalls, interlocking spurs. **Middle course:** wider valley, meanders with erosion on the outside bend and deposition on the inside. **Lower course:** flat floodplain, levees, oxbow lakes, and a **delta** or estuary at the mouth. Rivers such as the Sanaga and Wouri drain Cameroon to the Atlantic.

blocks.caption: A river’s long profile is steep near the source and gentle near the mouth.
blocks.alt: A curved line falling steeply then flattening, divided into upper, middle and lower course.

blocks.title: Reading a hydrograph
blocks.md: A **storm hydrograph** plots river discharge against time after rain. **Lag time** is the time between peak rainfall and peak discharge. A short lag time and steep rising limb mean a flashy, flood-prone river: steep slopes, impermeable rock, saturated soil, little vegetation and urban surfaces all shorten the lag.

blocks.title: Mistakes to avoid
blocks.md:
- A meander bend is eroded on the outside and has deposition on the inside, not the reverse.
- An oxbow lake is a cut-off meander, not a type of delta.
- Lag time is peak rainfall to peak discharge, not the length of the whole storm.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Lag time
blocks.statement: Peak rainfall was at 10:00 and peak discharge at 16:00. Find the lag time. A town stream peaks 2 hours after rain; say which is flashier and why.
steps: Lag time = 16:00 − 10:00 = 6 hours.
The town stream has a lag of 2 hours, which is shorter.
Concrete and drains carry water quickly to the channel: little infiltration.
blocks.answer: 6 hours; the urban stream is flashier because of impermeable surfaces.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Explain an oxbow lake
blocks.statement: Describe how an oxbow lake forms.
steps: Erosion on the outside of a meander and deposition on the inside make the loop narrower.
In a flood the river cuts through the neck of the loop.
Deposition seals the ends of the old loop.
The cut-off loop remains as a curved lake.
blocks.answer: A meander neck is cut through in flood and the abandoned loop is sealed off.

exercises.prompt: Describe and explain the features found at a destructive plate boundary where oceanic crust meets continental crust.
exercises.model: The denser oceanic plate is subducted beneath the continental plate, forming a deep ocean trench. Friction and melting produce magma, which rises to form volcanoes on the continental plate. Compression crumples sediments into fold mountains. The sticking and sudden slipping of the plates causes strong earthquakes, some deep. Subduction destroys oceanic crust.
exercises.rubric: Trench and subduction explained (1); magma/volcanoes (1); fold mountains (1); earthquakes with cause (1).
exercises.explanation: The denser oceanic plate is subducted beneath the continental plate, forming a deep ocean trench. The sticking and sudden slipping of the plates causes strong earthquakes, some deep. Subduction destroys oceanic crust.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Describe the main types of mass movement and explain the factors that cause them.
exercises.model: Mass movements include creep (slow), mudflow (wet, fluid), slump and landslide (blocks of material sliding) and rockfall (free fall from cliffs). They happen where gravity overcomes resistance. Steepness increases the downslope force. Water adds weight and lowers friction. Vegetation loss, undercutting and earthquakes can trigger movement. Weak, weathered rock fails more easily.
exercises.rubric: Types described (2); factors named (2); links explained (1).
exercises.explanation: Mass movements include creep (slow), mudflow (wet, fluid), slump and landslide (blocks of material sliding) and rockfall (free fall from cliffs). They happen where gravity overcomes resistance. Steepness increases the downslope force. Water adds weight and lowers friction. Vegetation loss, undercutting and earthquakes can trigger movement. Weak, weathered rock fails more easily.
